---
title: "Bit Field Enums in C#"
---

Think of it like **checkboxes** vs **radio buttons**:

```
Traditional Enum = Radio Buttons     Bit Field Enum = Checkboxes
(pick ONE)                           (pick MANY)

    ○ HorseRadish                        ☑ Summer
    ● Radish        ← selected           ☑ Autumn
    ○ Turnip                             ☐ Winter
                                         ☐ Spring
```

A **bit field** (also called a "flag enum") is an enumeration where each value represents a single bit position, allowing you to **combine multiple values** into a single variable using bitwise operations.

::: {.callout-note appearance="default" collapse="true"}
Q: Explain what the "A bit field" is from these enums:

```csharp
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

// A traditional enumeration of some root vegetables.
public enum SomeRootVegetables
{
    HorseRadish,
    Radish,
    Turnip
}

// A bit field or flag enumeration of harvesting seasons.
[Flags]
public enum Seasons
{
    None = 0,
    Summer = 1,
    Autumn = 2,
    Winter = 4,
    Spring = 8,
    All = Summer | Autumn | Winter | Spring
}
```
:::

## Traditional Enum vs Bit Field Enum

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        TRADITIONAL ENUM                                     │
│                     (SomeRootVegetables)                                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Can hold ONLY ONE value at a time                                          │
│                                                                             │
│  HorseRadish = 0                                                            │
│  Radish      = 1                                                            │
│  Turnip      = 2                                                            │
│                                                                             │
│  var veg = SomeRootVegetables.Radish;  // Just "Radish", nothing else       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         BIT FIELD ENUM                                      │
│                    [Flags] Seasons                                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Can hold MULTIPLE values combined together                                 │
│                                                                             │
│  var harvest = Seasons.Summer | Seasons.Autumn;  // "Summer, Autumn"        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```


## Why Powers of 2?

Each value must be a **power of 2** so that each occupies a unique bit position:

```
Value      Decimal    Binary (8-bit)
─────────────────────────────────────
None    =    0        0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
Summer  =    1        0 0 0 0 0 0 0 1
Autumn  =    2        0 0 0 0 0 0 1 0
Winter  =    4        0 0 0 0 0 1 0 0
Spring  =    8        0 0 0 0 1 0 0 0
                              ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑
                              │ │ │ └── Summer bit
                              │ │ └──── Autumn bit
                              │ └────── Winter bit
                              └──────── Spring bit
```


## How Combining Works (Bitwise OR `|`)

```
Summer | Autumn = ?

  Summer:   0 0 0 0 0 0 0 1
  Autumn:   0 0 0 0 0 0 1 0
            ─────────────────  (OR each column)
  Result:   0 0 0 0 0 0 1 1   = 3 (decimal)

This single number "3" represents BOTH Summer AND Autumn!
```

```
All = Summer | Autumn | Winter | Spring

  Summer:   0 0 0 0 0 0 0 1
  Autumn:   0 0 0 0 0 0 1 0
  Winter:   0 0 0 0 0 1 0 0
  Spring:   0 0 0 0 1 0 0 0
            ─────────────────
  All:      0 0 0 0 1 1 1 1   = 15 (decimal)
```


## Practical Example

```csharp
// Combine multiple seasons
Seasons harvestTime = Seasons.Summer | Seasons.Autumn;

Console.WriteLine(harvestTime);           // Output: "Summer, Autumn"
Console.WriteLine((int)harvestTime);      // Output: 3

// Check if a specific flag is set (using HasFlag)
if (harvestTime.HasFlag(Seasons.Summer))
{
    Console.WriteLine("Harvest in summer!");  // This prints
}

if (harvestTime.HasFlag(Seasons.Winter))
{
    Console.WriteLine("Harvest in winter!");  // This does NOT print
}

// Add a season (bitwise OR)
harvestTime |= Seasons.Spring;
Console.WriteLine(harvestTime);           // Output: "Summer, Autumn, Spring"

// Remove a season (bitwise AND with NOT)
harvestTime &= ~Seasons.Summer;
Console.WriteLine(harvestTime);           // Output: "Autumn, Spring"
```


## The `[Flags]` Attribute

The `[Flags]` attribute tells the compiler:

1. This enum is intended to be used as a bit field
2. When you call `.ToString()`, it should display combined values nicely (e.g., `"Summer, Autumn"` instead of just `"3"`)

```csharp
// Without [Flags]: prints "3"
// With [Flags]:    prints "Summer, Autumn"
```


## Real-World Analogy


This is commonly used for things like:

- File permissions (Read, Write, Execute)
- UI options (Bold, Italic, Underline)
- Days of the week
- Feature flags
